newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: World's largest bank registered in New Zealand.
newsitem.headline: World's largest bank registered in New Zealand.

text.p: Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi, the world's largest bank, has registered in New Zealand as a bank mainly to expand its corporate business, a spokesman said on Wednesday.
The bank, which has had a representative office in New Zealand since 1972, was registered via its wholly-owned subsidiary, Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi (Australia) Ltd, by the Reserve Bank on Wednesday.
It will be the only Japanese bank of 17 registered here.

"We consider the priority is to exchange business with Japanese corporates based in New Zealand. We would like to support those who have newly extended their business into the New Zealand market," Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi's New Zealand spokesman Keiji Miyoshi told Reuters.
"This business will become the basis of our branch.
"Also, we'd like to expand our existing business with major New Zealand companies and multi-national companies in New Zealand," he said.
Miyoshi said the company had identified opportunities in the energy and forestry sectors.
He said that tax reforms in New Zealand in 1991 were a major catalyst to Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi's business here.
Japan is New Zealand's second largest export market after Australia.
The bank, which will initially be a small operation with just nine staff, will also establish forex operations to take advantage of New Zealand's time zone as the first market in the world to open.
"New Zealand financial forex markets open earliest in the world and it is meaningful to have a branch here to take advantage of this," said Miyoshi.
He said the bank had registered in New Zealand via the Australian branch rather than through the head office in order to have a unified management structure in this region.
Banking analysts said the decision by Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi to register was significant.
Japanese banks and investors shunned New Zealand in the wake of the collapse of DFC New Zealand in 1989 owing more than NZ$2 billion, mainly to Japanese banks and investors.

Most of the Japanese investors erroneously believed loans to the former state-owned DFC were government guaranteed. However, all major DFC debtors were repaid from recoveries and the attitude of Japanese investors towards New Zealand softened.
Miyoshi said that the issue of DFC was not a barrier to Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi registering in New Zealand.
Registration in New Zealand is the first major move offshore for Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi since Bank of Tokyo and Mitsubishi Bank merged on April 1, 1996 to create the world's largest bank by assets.
At least one other bank, Sumitomo Bank Ltd has shown interest in Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi's move in New Zealand.
However, Miyoshi said the old days of all Japanese banks matching each other's moves were over.
"I don't think that because one bank registers, other Japanese banks will follow. That is an old story."
